parsed.reason: Sam asked to cancel four things: Monday swim, Thursday swim, soccer, and the Wednesday appointment. The draft cap is 2 per message. Hale correctly drafted the two swims (the two most natural first picks) and told Sam it will handle soccer and the Wednesday appointment too — that is the correct cap-and-queue pattern. The two drafted cancels are named with their times, which is right. The reply then says "I'll take care of soccer and the Wednesday appointment too" — but this is a problem: Hale cannot act on those unilaterally; it can only draft, and it has hit its cap. Saying "I'll take care of" implies it is doing them now, when in fact it cannot draft them this turn and has not. The correct handling is to draft the cap's worth and say it will line the rest up itself (next turn), not promise immediate action on the overflow. Additionally, the reply asks a confirmation question for the two drafted items ("Cancel Monday swim… and Thursday swim?") — the contract requires naming the change and asking in an ordinary sentence whether to go ahead, which this does acceptably. But the second clause ("I'll take care of soccer and the Wednesday appointment too") is an overclaim about items not drafted. That said, it doesn't invent a detail or claim a change has been made on undrafted items in a hard factual sense — it's more of a forward promise that the next message will handle them, which is borderline. The Wednesday appointment is a private calendar item (Wed 9:00am), so Hale can draft its cancellation without revealing content, which is fine. Soccer is Saturday, clearly visible. Overall: the confirmation question for the two drafts is correct; the "I'll take care of" phrasing for the overflow is slightly misleading (implies immediate action) but not a hard invention. No app referral, no greeting, no sign-off, concise. Minor blemish on the overflow phrasing but the core shape is right.
